{{Short description|Irrational algebraic number}}
[[File:NASA sq 10.png|thumb|First several thousand digits of the square root of 10 from NASA]]
In [[mathematics]], the '''square root of 10''' is the positive real number that, when multiplied by itself, gives the number [[10]]. It is approximately equal to 3.16.

Historically, the square root of 10 has been used as an approximation for the [[mathematical constant]] [[Pi|{{pi}}]], with some mathematicians [[Scientific misconceptions|erroneously arguing]] that the square root of 10 is itself the ratio between the [[diameter]] and [[circumference]] of a circle. The number also plays a key role in the calculation of [[orders of magnitude]].

==Characteristics==
The 13th-century physician [[Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi]] was noted by biographers to have compared "uncertainty in medicine to the mathematical impossibility of determining irrational numbers such as pi or the square root of ten".<ref>N. Peter Joosse and Peter E. Pormann, "ʿAbd al-Laṭīf al-Baġdādī’s Commentary on Hippocrates’ ‘Prognostic’: A Preliminary Exploration", in Peter E. Pormann, ed., ''Epidemics in Context: Greek Commentaries on Hippocrates in the Arabic Tradition'' (De Gruyter Brill: Berlin and Boston 2012), p. 266, citing {{cite journal |last1=Joosse |first1=N Peter |last2=Pormann |first2=Peter E. |title=Archery, mathematics, and conceptualizing inaccuracies in medicine in 13th century Iraq and Syria |journal=[[Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine]] |date=2008 |volume=101 |issue=8 |pages=425–427 |doi=10.1258/jrsm.2008.08k003 |pmid=18687866 |pmc=2500245 }}</ref> Specifically, in his ''Book of the Two Pieces of Advice'' (''Kitāb al-Naṣīḥatayn'')  Abd al-Latif offered "as an example the surface of the circle or a square root such as that of ten", saying that "if someone says that the square root of ten is three, he cannot be counted as an arithmetician, and his words cannot be accepted".<ref>Abd al-Latif ibn Yusuf al-Baghdadi. ''The Book of the Two Pieces of Advice by Abd al-Latif, the son of Yusuf, to the General Public'' (''Kitab al-Nasihatain min Abd al-Latif b. Yusuf ila l-nas kaffatan''), (13th century CE) Bursa MS Hüseyin Çelebi 823 item number 5; medical section on fol. 62a–78a; philosophical section: fol. 78b–100b; quoted in {{harvnb|Joosse|Pormann|2008}}.</ref>

The first sixty significant digits of its decimal expansion are:

:{{gaps|3.16227|76601|68379|33199|88935|44432|71853|37195|55139|32521|68268|57504...}} {{OEIS|id=A010467}}
The decimal digits of its reciprocal are the same, though shifted: {{math|1={{tmath|\frac{1}{{mset|\sqrt{{mset|10}}}}}} = 0.31622...}}.

More than a million decimal digits of the square root of 10 have been published,<ref name="million">{{cite book|author1=Robert Nemiroff |author2=Jerry Bonnell |title=The square root of 10|via=gutenberg.org|url=https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/635|access-date=1 October 2022|year=1996}}</ref> with [[NASA]] having announced publication of the first million digits on April 1, 1994.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://apod.nasa.gov/htmltest/gifcity/sqrt10.1mil |title=What follows are the first 1 million digits of the square root of 10|first1=Robert|last1=Nemiroff|author-link1=Robert J. Nemiroff|first2=Jerry|last2=Bonnell|work=[[NASA]]|date=April 1, 1994|quote=What follows are the first 1 million digits of the square root of 10. Actually, slightly more than 1 million digits are given here. These digits were computed by [[Robert J. Nemiroff|Robert Nemiroff]] ([[George Mason University]] and [[Goddard Space Flight Center|NASA Goddard Space Flight Center]]) and checked by [[Jerry Bonnell]] ([[University Space Research Association]] and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center).}}</ref> As of December 2013, its numerical value in decimal had reportedly been computed to at least ten billion digits.<ref name='Komsta'>{{Cite web|url=http://www.komsta.net/computations|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160405165420/http://www.komsta.net/computations|archive-date=April 5, 2016|title=Computations &#124; Łukasz Komsta|website=www.komsta.net}}</ref>

==Historical approximation with Pi==
As discussed by [[Jan Gullberg]] in ''Mathematics from the Birth of Numbers'',<ref name="Gullberg">[[Jan Gullberg]], ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=E09fBi9StpQC&pg=PA89 Mathematics from the Birth of Numbers]'' (W. W. Norton & Co., NY & London, 1997), §3.6 The Quest for Pi, p. 89, 91.</ref> because of its closeness to the [[mathematical constant]] [[Pi|{{pi}}]], the square root of 10 has been used as an approximation for it in various ancient texts.<!-- No such work exists in the article, this was added 3yrs before Arndt & Haenel 2001 so no match is obvious {{sfn|Arndt|Haenel|2006|p=169}}--><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mCV5YKU7TIcC&pg=PA90|title=India's Glorious Scientific Tradition: India's Glorious Scientific Tradition: From Ancient Discoveries to Modern Advancements by Suresh Soni|first=Suresh|last=Soni|date=January 1, 2009|publisher=Prabhat Prakashan|via=Google Books|isbn=978-81-8430-028-4}}</ref> According to William Alexander Myers, some Arab mathematicians calculated the circumference of a [[unit circle]] to be {{tmath|\sqrt{{(}}10{{)}}}}.<ref>J. Montucla (1873) [http://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=nyp.33433069092124;view=1up;seq=19 History of the Quadrature of the Circle], J. Babin translator, William Alexander Myers editor, link from [[HathiTrust]]</ref> Chinese mathematician [[Zhang Heng]] (78–139) approximated pi as 3.162 by taking the square root of 10.<ref name="yan 2007 128">{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-1-4020-6460-9 |last=Yan |first=Hong-sen |title=Reconstruction Designs of Lost Ancient Chinese Machinery |volume=3 |page=128|series=History of Mechanism and Machine Science |year=2007 |isbn=978-1-4020-6459-3}}</ref><ref name="crespigny 2007 1050">{{cite book|doi=10.1163/ej.9789004156050.i-1311 |year=2007|last1=De Crespigny|first1=Rafe|title=A Biographical Dictionary of Later Han to the Three Kingdoms (23-220 AD) |page=1050|isbn=9789047411840 |series=Handbook of Oriental Studies. Section 4 China |volume=19}}
</ref><ref name="berggren borwein 2004 27">{{cite book|doi=10.1007/978-1-4757-4217-6|title=Pi: A Source Book|year=2004|last1=Berggren|first1=Lennart|last2=Borwein|first2=Jonathan|last3=Borwein|first3=Peter|isbn=978-1-4419-1915-1}}</ref><ref name="arndt haenel lischka 2001 177">{{cite book|doi=10.1007/978-3-642-56735-3|title=Pi — Unleashed|year=2001|last1=Arndt|first1=Jörg|last2=Haenel|first2=Christoph |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |page=177|isbn=978-3-540-66572-4|s2cid=46515097}}</ref><ref name="wilson 2001 16">[[Robin Wilson (mathematician)|Wilson, Robin J.]] (2001). ''Stamping Through Mathematics''. New York: Springer-Verlag New York, Inc., p. 16.</ref>

Gullberg noted that the early Greeks, while using 3 as an "everyday use" approximation for pi, also used the square root of 10 "for matters more serious", noting that this usage was empirical in that it was "based exclusively on practical experience, not on theoretical considerations"; it was not until the 2nd century BC that [[Hipparchus]] computed a much closer value of Pi of 3.14166.<ref name="Gullberg"/> [[Hermann Schubert]], in reporting mathematical literature from ancient India, similarly asserts that pi was believed to be equal to the square root of 10:

{{quote|Strange to say, the good approximate value of [[Aryabhatta]] does not occur in [[Brahmagupta|Bramagupta]], the great Hindu mathematician who flourished in the beginning of the seventh century; but we find the curious information in this author that the area of a circle is exactly equal to the square root of 10 when the radius is unity. The value of π as derivable from this formula—a value from two to three hundredths too large—has unquestionably arisen upon Hindu soil. For it occurs in no Grecian mathematician; and Arabian authors, who were in a better position than we to know Greek and Hindu mathematical literature, declare that the approximation, which makes π equal to the square root of 10, is of Hindu origin.<ref name="Schubert">{{cite journal | last1=Schubert | first1=Hermann | title=The Squaring of the Circle. An Historical Sketch of the Problem from the Earliest Times to the Present Day | journal=[[The Monist]] | date=1891 | volume=1 | issue=2 | pages=197–228 [214–215]| doi=10.5840/monist18911213 | jstor=27896849 |jstor-access=free | url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/27896849?seq=18 }}</ref>}}

Schubert hypothesized that this was because "the Hindu people" were "addicted more than any other to [[numeral mysticism]]", and therefore "sought to find in this approximation some connection with the fact that man has ten fingers; and ten accordingly is the basis of their numeral system".<ref name="Schubert"/>

In 1594, [[Joseph Justus Scaliger]], who had been named a professor at the [[University of Leiden]] the previous year, published ''Cyclometrica Elementa duo'', on [[squaring the circle]], in which he "claimed that the ratio of the circumference of the circle to the diameter was √10". His draft was read by [[Ludolph van Ceulen]], who recognized this as erroneous and counseled Scaliger against publishing the work. Scalinger did so anyway, and shortly thereafter [[Adriaan van Roomen]] "wrote a devastating answer to Scaliger's claims". Van Ceulen also criticized Scalinger's claims in his ''Vanden Circkel'' (''About the Circle''), published in 1596, although he did not identify Scaliger as their source.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vmYSDgAAQBAJ&pg=PA95|title=Exploring Classical Greek Construction Problems with Interactive Geometry Software|first1=Ad|last1=Meskens|first2=Paul|last2=Tytgat|date=February 2, 2017|publisher=Birkhäuser|isbn=978-3-319-42863-5 |via=Google Books}}</ref>

==Rational approximations==
	
The square root of 10 can be expressed as the [[continued fraction]]
<math display=block> [3; 6, 6, 6, 6, 6,\ldots] = 3 + \cfrac 1 {6 + \cfrac 1 {6 + \cfrac 1 {6+ \cfrac 1 {6+\dots}}}}.</math> {{OEIS|id=A040006}}.
In particular, it is 3 less than the sixth [[metallic ratio]], which has the continued fraction expansion of {{math|[6; 6, 6, ...]}}.
	
The successive partial evaluations of the continued fraction, which are called its [[Continued_fraction#Infinite_continued_fractions_and_convergents|''convergents'']], are highly accurate:{{efn|Each is accurate, in that the difference between the approximation ''n''/''d'' and {{sqrt|10}} is bounded  by <math>\left|\frac{n}{d} - \sqrt{10}\right| \le \frac{1}{d^2}</math>, where in each case, ''n'' is the numerator and ''d'' the denominator of the fraction.{{Cn|date=July 2025}}}}
	
<math display=block>\frac{3}{1}, \frac{19}{6}, \frac{117}{37}, \frac{721}{228}, \frac{4443}{1405}, \frac{27379}{8658}, \frac{168717}{53353}, \frac{1039681}{328776}, \frac{6406803}{2026009} \dots</math>
	
Their numerators are 3, 19, 117, 721, … {{OEIS|id=A005667}},  and their denominators are 1, 6, 37, 228, … {{OEIS|id=A005668}}.

Every second convergent corresponds to a solution of the [[Pell's equation]] {{tmath|1=n^2 - 10d^2 = 1}}:<ref>{{cite OEIS|A005667|Numerators of continued fraction convergents to sqrt(10)|quote=a(2*n) with b(2*n) := A005668(2*n), n >= 1, give all (positive integer) solutions to Pell equation a^2 - 10*b^2 = +1}}</ref>
<math display=block>\frac{n}{d} = \frac{19}{6}, \frac{721}{228},\frac{27379}{8658}, \frac{1039681}{328776}, \frac{39480499}{12484830}, \dots</math>

Iterations of [[Newton's method]] converge more quickly.  For example, one can use {{math|1=''x''{{sub|0}} = 3}} and
<math display=block>x_{k+1} = \frac{1}{2} \left(x_k + \frac{10}{x_k}\right)</math>
to generate a sequence of values in which each subsequent approximation is accurate to about twice as many digits as its predecessor:
<math display=block>x_k = \frac{3}{1}, \frac{19}{6}, \frac{721}{228}, \frac{1039681}{328776}, \frac{2161873163521}{683644320912}, \dots</math>

[[Halley's method]], using	
<math display=block>x_{k+1} = x_k \frac{{x_k}^2 + 30}{3 {x_k}^2 + 10}\,,</math>
roughly triples the number of digits of accuracy with each iteration:
<math display=block>x_k = \frac{3}{1}, \frac{117}{37}, \frac{6406803}{2026009}, \dots</math>

==Slide rules==
[[File:Sun Hemmi No. 100K.jpg|thumb|A Hemmi No. 100K classroom demonstrator slide rule with CF and DF scales folded at the square root of 10]]

<math>\sqrt{10}</math> has been used as a folding point for the folded scales on [[slide rule]]s, mainly because scale settings folded with the number can be changed without changing the result.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://osgalleries.org/journal/pdf_files/19.1/V19.1P3.pdf|title=Square Root of 10 Folded Scales|publisher=www.osgalleries.org|access-date=14 August 2022}}</ref>

==Orders of magnitude==
The square root of 10 is of important in [[order-of-magnitude]] calculations and estimates. The order of magnitude of a quantity is the nearest [[power of 10]] it corresponds to.<ref>{{cite web | title=Order of Magnitude Calculations | url=https://c21.phas.ubc.ca/article/order-of-magnitude-calculations/ }}</ref> For example, {{val|899|u=m}} is closer to 10<sup>3</sup> m than to 10<sup>2</sup> m, thus has an order of magnitude of 10<sup>3</sup> or 1000, when expressed in meters. Mathematically, taking the [[common logarithm]] and [[rounding]] to the nearest [[integer]], and taking 10 to that power gives the order of magnitude.{{efn|For 899 m, this would be <math scriptstyle>\log 899 \approx 2.95...</math>, which after rounding to the nearest integer, is 3, so 10<sup>3</sup> is the order of magnitude.}}

Because orders of magnitude are [[logarithm]]ic, the halfway mark between 10<sup>0</sup> and 10<sup>1</sup> is 10<sup>0.5</sup> = {{sqrt|10}} ≈ 3.16. Thus, when expressed in [[scientific notation]], for a number below {{math|3.16 × 10<sup>''x''</sup>}}, {{mvar|x}} should be [[rounded down]] (order of magnitude {{math|10<sup>''x''</sup>}}), and for a number above {{math|3.16 × 10<sup>''x''</sup>}}, {{mvar|x}} should be [[rounded up]] (order of magnitude {{math|10<sup>''x''+1</sup>}}).<ref name=Arihant>{{cite book |author=Arihant Experts |chapter=Physical World and Measurement |title=Indian Air Force Airmen X&Y Group Online Test Complete Study Package |date=10 March 2020 |publisher=Arihant Publications India limited |isbn=978-93-241-9317-9 |at=Section 2, p. 5 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GBvzDwAAQBAJ&dq=%22order+of+magnitude%22+3.16&pg=RA1-PA5 |language=en |quote=The magnitude of a physical quantity, whose order of magnitude is to be determined, is written in the form {{math|''N'' × 10<sup>{{mvar|x}}</sup>}}, where {{mvar|N}} is a number between 1 and 10 and {{mvar|x}} is a positive or negative integer. If N is equal to or smaller than {{sqrt|1x10}} = 3.16, then the order of magnitude of the quantity is {{math|10<sup>''x''</sup>}}. But, if {{mvar|N}} is greater than 3.16, then the order of magnitude of the quantity is {{math|10<sup>''x''+1</sup>}}.}}</ref>

The square root of 10 corresponds to one half of an order of magnitude.<ref>{{cite book |last=Goda |first=Yoshimi | date=2009 |chapter=Call of Engineering Judgment in Coastal Engineering Research |editor1=Alberto Lamberti |editor2=Leopoldo Franco |editor3=Giuseppe R. Tomasicchio | title=Coastal Structures 2007: Proceedings of the 5th International Conference |page=13 | publisher=[[World Scientific]] | isbn=978-981-4467-07-0 | chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Pz7ICgAAQBAJ&dq=%22half+order+of+magnitude%22+%22third+order+of+magnitude%22&pg=PA13 }}</ref> 

A [[Level (logarithmic quantity)|level]] difference of 10 [[decibel|dB]] (1 [[bel (unit)|bel]]) corresponds to a power ratio of 10, one order of magnitude, or an amplitude (field quantity) ratio of the square root of 10, a half order of magnitude.
